claim: MKK6 KO mice have reduced body weight compared to age-matched wild type animals.
source: Mice lacking MKK6 have reduced body weight compared to age-matched wild type (WT) animals (Figure 1A and B)
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 1B comparing WT and MKK6 KO mice over time.

claim: MKK6 KO mice have a dramatic reduction in white adipose tissue.
source: which can be partially explained by a dramatic reduction in white adipose tissue (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by measurements of white adipose tissue to tibia length ratio shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MKK6 KO mice are protected against diet-induced obesity with increased browning of the epididymal white adipose tissue.
source: This agrees with previous studies demonstrating that MKK6 KO mice are protected against diet-induced obesity with increased browning of the epididymal white adipose tissue (Matesanz et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matesanz et al., 2017.

claim: MKK6 KO mice exhibit an abnormal posture characterized by a hunched position and the development of thoracic kyphosis.
source: Additionally, these mice exhibit an abnormal posture characterized by a hunched position and the development of thoracic kyphosis and severe ataxia (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by CT scan images and kyphosis angle quantification shown in Figure 1D.

claim: MKK6 KO mice exhibit severe ataxia.
source: Additionally, these mice exhibit an abnormal posture characterized by a hunched position and the development of thoracic kyphosis and severe ataxia (Figure 1D, Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to video documentation (Figure 1—video 1).

claim: MKK6 KO mice suffer premature death with the first mice dying at 51 weeks of age and a median lifespan of 76 weeks.
source: As a consequence of all these phenotypic alterations, MKK6 KO mice suffer premature death, the first mice dying at 51 weeks of age with a median lifespan of 76 weeks (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival plot shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Combined deletion of p38α and p38β results in cardiac defects during embryonic development.
source: Combined deletion of p38α and p38β results in cardiac defects during embryonic development (del Barco Barrantes et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to del Barco Barrantes et al., 2011.

claim: p38γ/δ deficient mice exhibit reduced cardiomyocyte hypertrophic growth and smaller hearts.
source: whereas p38γ/δ deficient mice exhibit reduced cardiomyocyte hypertrophic growth and smaller hearts (González-Terán et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: Cardiovascular disease is a common characteristic in premature aging syndromes.
source: and cardiovascular disease is a common characteristic in premature aging syndromes (Carrero et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carrero et al., 2016.

claim: 12-14-month-old MKK6 KO mice demonstrate eccentric hypertrophy compared to control mice.
source: Echocardiographic analyses of 12–14-month-old mice demonstrated eccentric hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice compared to control mice, as detected by thinning of the left ventricle (LV) wall, as well as increased left ventricular internal diameter and left ventricular volume, especially during the systole (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cardiac enlargement in 12-14-month-old MKK6 KO mice compromises systolic function, evidenced by a decrease in the ejection fraction and fractional shortening.
source: Cardiac enlargement compromised systolic function, evidenced by a decrease in the ejection fraction and fractional shortening.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Diastolic function appears to be maintained in 12-14-month-old MKK6 KO mice, with a normal E/A wave velocities ratio and isovolumetric relaxation time.
source: However, the diastolic function appeared to be maintained, with a normal E/A wave velocities ratio and isovolumetric relaxation time (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MKK6 KO mice exhibit bradycardia.
source: Moreover, MKK6 KO mice exhibit bradycardia (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by heart rate measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: MKK6 KO old mice have cardiac fibrotic lesions.
source: We performed picrosirius red staining for collagen and quantified positive areas in serial histologic sections from MKK6 KO and WT hearts and found cardiac fibrotic lesions in MKK6 KO old mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by picrosirius red staining and quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MKK6 KO mice do not present differences in blood pressure compared to age-matched controls.
source: MKK6 KO mice did not present differences in blood pressure compared to age-matched controls (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by blood pressure measurements shown in Figure 2E.

claim: 9-week-old MKK6-deficient animals demonstrate cardiac hypertrophy when compared with controls.
source: Echocardiographic analysis at 9 weeks of age demonstrated cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6-deficient animals when compared with controls, as detected by measures of left ventricular mass, interventricular septal thickness, left ventricular posterior wall thickness, and left ventricular internal diameter (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Cardiac enlargement in 9-week-old MKK6 KO mice does not compromise systolic or diastolic function.
source: However, cardiac enlargement did not compromise systolic or diastolic function (given by the ejection fraction and the E/A wave velocity ratio, respectively) but was accompanied by an increase in stroke volume and cardiac output (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cardiac enlargement in 9-week-old MKK6 KO mice is accompanied by an increase in stroke volume and cardiac output.
source: However, cardiac enlargement did not compromise systolic or diastolic function (given by the ejection fraction and the E/A wave velocity ratio, respectively) but was accompanied by an increase in stroke volume and cardiac output (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MKK6-deficient hearts are larger than WT controls when normalized to tibia length.
source: Gross anatomic and histologic analyses confirmed that these non-invasive findings as MKK6-deficient hearts were larger than WT controls when normalized to tibia length (TL) (Figure 3C&D)
evidence: Supported by heart weight to tibia length ratio measurements shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: The difference in heart size between MKK6 KO and WT mice is not apparent at 4 weeks of age.
source: a difference that was not apparent at 4 weeks of age.
evidence: Inferred from the serial analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Serial analysis of heart weight/tibia length over 15 weeks demonstrates enhanced cardiac growth in MKK6 KO mice.
source: Serial analysis of heart weight (HW)/TL over 15 weeks demonstrated enhanced cardiac growth in MKK6 KO mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by serial measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The progressive increase in the size of MKK6 KO hearts correlates with increased cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area.
source: The progressive increase in the size of MKK6 KO hearts correlated with increased cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area, consistent with enhanced hypertrophic growth (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claim: MKK6 KO mice demonstrate reduced systolic blood pressures when compared to age-matched controls.
source: Hypertension was excluded as a possible contributor to this increased growth as MKK6 KO mice demonstrate reduced systolic blood pressures when compared to age-matched controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by blood pressure measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Histological cardiac examination reveals no evidence of fibrosis in 9-week-old MKK6 KO heart sections.
source: Histological cardiac examination revealed no evidence of fibrosis in MKK6 KO heart sections (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by picrosirius red staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is no difference in the expression of fibrotic genes including Col1a1, Col3a1, and Fn in 9-week-old MKK6 KO hearts.
source: We also found no difference in the expression of fibrotic genes including Col1a1, Col3a1, and Fn or markers of the fetal gene program (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is no difference in the expression of markers of the fetal gene program in 9-week-old MKK6 KO hearts.
source: We also found no difference in the expression of fibrotic genes including Col1a1, Col3a1, and Fn or markers of the fetal gene program (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: No meaningful changes are visible for Nppa or Nppb in 9-week-old MKK6 KO hearts.
source: No meaningful changes were visible for Nppa or Nppb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At 9 weeks of age, MKK6 KO hearts show a non-pathological cardiac hypertrophy.
source: These observations suggest that at 9 weeks of age, MKK6 KO hearts show a non-pathological cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of fibrosis and fetal gene program reactivation in 9-week-old MKK6 KO hearts.

claim: The cardiac phenotype of 9-week-old MKK6MCK-KO mice resembles that of MKK6 KO animals.
source: Importantly, the cardiac phenotype of 9-weeks-old MKK6MCK−KO mice resembled that of MKK6 KO animals (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by heart weight, histology, and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Similar results to MKK6MCK-KO mice were obtained with Myh6-Cre; Map2k6LoxP/LoxP (MKK6αMHC-KO) mice.
source: Similar results were obtained with Myh6-Cre; Map2k6LoxP/LoxP (MKK6αMHC−KO) mice (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: Supported by heart weight, histology, and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Cardiomyocyte MKK6 controls heart growth.
source: These data collectively confirm that cardiomyocyte MKK6 controls heart growth.
evidence: Inferred from the cardiac hypertrophy phenotype observed in cardiomyocyte-specific MKK6 knockout mice.

claim: MKK6αMHC-KO mice show a reduced survival, with a median lifespan of 51 weeks.
source: Similar to the whole-body MKK6 KO animals, MKK6αMHC−KO mice showed a reduced survival, with a median lifespan of 51 weeks (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival plot shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The increased mortality in MKK6αMHC-KO mice is accompanied by cardiac dilatation and cardiac dysfunction.
source: This increased mortality was accompanied by cardiac dilatation and cardiac dysfunction, as revealed by echocardiographic analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by echocardiography measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: MKK6 KO hearts demonstrate hyperphosphorylation of p38γ and p38δ.
source: We assessed the relative levels of phosphorylated p38 isoforms by immunoprecipitation in MKK6 KO hearts, which demonstrated hyperphosphorylation of p38γ and p38δ (Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: MKK6 KO hearts show a reduction in phosphorylation of p38α.
source: with a simultaneous reduction in phosphorylation of p38α (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MKK6 KO hearts show increased levels of phosphorylated MKK3.
source: Immunoblot analysis also revealed increased levels of phosphorylated MKK3, the other main p38 upstream activator, in MKK6 KO hearts (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of p38γ and p38δ in the MKK6 KO hearts results from MKK3 activation.
source: This observation suggested that increased phosphorylation of p38γ and p38δ in the MKK6 KO hearts resulted from MKK3 activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased MKK3 phosphorylation and p38γ/δ hyperphosphorylation in MKK6 KO hearts.

claim: Phosphorylation of p38γ and p38δ is strongly reduced in MKK3-deficient mice.
source: Accordingly, phosphorylation of p38γ and p38δ was strongly reduced in MKK3-deficient mice, whereas p38α phosphorylation was not changed appreciably (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: p38α phosphorylation is not changed appreciably in MKK3-deficient mice.
source: Accordingly, phosphorylation of p38γ and p38δ was strongly reduced in MKK3-deficient mice, whereas p38α phosphorylation was not changed appreciably (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot analysis shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Hearts of MKK3 KO mice are smaller at 9 weeks of age when compared with age-matched WT controls.
source: In addition, hearts of MKK3 KO mice were smaller at 9 weeks of age when compared with age-matched WT controls (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by heart weight to tibia length ratio measurements shown in Figure 5E.

claim: p38γ and p38δ have previously been demonstrated to promote cardiac hypertrophic growth.
source: a finding consistent with the previously described roles of p38γ and p38δ in promoting postnatal cardiac hypertrophic growth (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: p38αMCK-KO mice present an increased expression and phosphorylation of MKK3 and MKK6.
source: p38αMCK-KO mice presented an increased expression and phosphorylation of MKK3 and MKK6 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: p38α regulates p38 upstream kinases at the transcriptional level.
source: This agreed with previous evidence indicating that p38α regulates p38 upstream kinases at the transcriptional level (Ambrosino et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ambrosino et al., 2003.

claim: Lack of p38α activation promotes an increase in MKK3 mRNA and protein levels in MKK6 KO mice.
source: We then evaluated MKK3 expression in hearts from MKK6 KO mice and found that lack of p38α activation also promoted an increase in MKK3 mRNA and protein levels in these animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C)
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B and C.

claim: There is a negative feedback regulation of MKK3 expression and activity by p38α activation.
source: indicating a negative feedback regulation of MKK3 expression and activity by p38α activation.
evidence: Inferred from the increased MKK3 expression and phosphorylation observed in p38α-deficient mice.

claim: In the heart, MKK6 primarily targets p38α and MKK3 targets p38γ and p38δ.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that in the heart, MKK6 primarily targets p38α and MKK3 targets p38γ and p38δ.
evidence: Inferred from the differential phosphorylation patterns of p38 isoforms in MKK3 and MKK6 knockout mice.

claim: MKK6 deficiency leads to cardiac hypertrophy via activation of MKK3 and p38γ and p38δ.
source: In addition, they suggest that MKK6 deficiency leads to cardiac hypertrophy via activation of MKK3 and p38γ and p38δ.
evidence: Inferred from the hyperactivation of MKK3-p38γ/δ pathway and cardiac hypertrophy phenotype in MKK6 KO mice.

claim: The double mutant combination (MKK6/p38γ DKO) rescues normal cardiac growth.
source: The double mutant combination (MKK6/p38γ DKO) rescued normal cardiac growth, as the heart sizes and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional areas of the double mutants were equivalent to those of WT controls (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by heart weight, histology, and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: MKK6-deficient hearts lacking p38δ in their myocytes are similar in size to those of mice lacking p38δ in their myocytes.
source: MKK6-deficient hearts lacking p38δ in their myocytes (MKK6 KO; Mck-Cre; Mapk13LoxP/LoxP [MKK6 KO/p38δMCK−KO]) were similar in size to those of mice lacking p38δ in their myocytes (Mck-Cre; Mapk13LoxP/LoxP [p38δMCK−KO]), with no appreciable increase in cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by heart weight, histology, and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Enhanced cardiac hypertrophic growth in MKK6-deficient mice is mediated by hyperactivation of p38γ/δ signaling in striated muscle.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that enhanced cardiac hypertrophic growth in MKK6-deficient mice is mediated by hyperactivation of p38γ/δ signaling in striated muscle.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice upon deletion of p38γ or p38δ.

claim: p38γ and p38δ isoforms promote cardiac hypertrophic growth through activation of mTOR signaling by targeting the mTOR-inhibitory protein DEPTOR for degradation.
source: The p38γ and p38δ isoforms have previously been demonstrated to promote cardiac hypertrophic growth through activation of mTOR signaling by targeting the mTOR-inhibitory protein DEPTOR for degradation (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: MKK6 KO mouse hearts show an increase in mTOR pathway activation.
source: As expected from that finding, immunoblot analysis of MKK6 KO mouse hearts showed an increase in mTOR pathway activation (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MKK6 KO mouse hearts show reduced levels of DEPTOR protein.
source: together with reduced levels of DEPTOR protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MKK6 KO hearts show an overall increase in translational activation.
source: We found an overall increase in translational activation in MKK6 KO hearts relative to WT (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis of eukaryotic initiation/elongation factors shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MKK6 KO hearts demonstrate greater puromycin labeling.
source: We corroborated these findings by analyzing puromycin incorporation into newly synthesized peptides in WT and MKK6 KO hearts, which demonstrated greater puromycin labeling (Figure 7C)
evidence: Supported by in vivo protein synthesis measurements shown in Figure 7C.

claim: MKK6 KO hearts have overall higher protein content.
source: and overall protein content (Figure 7D) in mutant hearts.
evidence: Supported by protein-DNA ratio measurements shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Rapamycin treatment is sufficient to bring the heart size of MKK6 KO animals close to that of WT age-matched controls.
source: This treatment was sufficient to bring the heart size (HW/TL) of MKK6 KO animals close to that of WT age-matched controls, which corresponded with a robust reduction in cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area in MKK6 KO mice (Figure 7E-G)
evidence: Supported by heart weight, histology, and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements after rapamycin treatment shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: The cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice results from hyperactivation of mTOR signaling.
source: altogether suggesting that the cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice results from hyperactivation of mTOR signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue of cardiac hypertrophy by rapamycin treatment.

claim: MKK6-deficient MEFs show mTOR pathway activation and increased cell size.
source: Namely, MKK6-deficient MEFs showed mTOR pathway activation and increased cell size (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by cell area quantification and immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Lentiviral infection of MEFs with an active form of p38α is able to reduce mTOR pathway activity as well as cell size.
source: Furthermore, lentiviral infection of MEFs with an active form of p38α (D176A/F327S) was able to reduce mTOR pathway activity as well as cell size (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by cell area quantification and immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: MKK3 deletion in the context of MKK6 deficiency promotes a reduction in the phosphorylation of p38γ as well as in mTOR pathway activity.
source: We found that MKK3 deletion in the context of MKK6 deficiency promoted a reduction in the phosphorylation of p38γ as well as in mTOR pathway activity (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: MKK3 deletion in the context of MKK6 deficiency is accompanied by an attenuation in the heart growth of MKK3/6MCK-KO animals.
source: This was accompanied by an attenuation in the heart growth of MKK3/6MCK-KO animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 3C)
evidence: Supported by heart weight measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: MKK3 deletion in the context of MKK6 deficiency is not sufficient to revert heart growth to the level of MCK-Cre control animals.
source: although it was not sufficient to revert it to the level of MCK-Cre control animals.
evidence: Supported by heart weight measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Lack of MKK6 reduces the lifespan in mice.
source: Here, we demonstrate that lack of MKK6 reduces the lifespan in mice.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Young MKK6 KO mice develop cardiac hypertrophy which progresses to cardiac dilatation and fibrosis with age.
source: Longitudinal study of cardiac function in MKK6 KO mice showed that young mice develop cardiac hypertrophy which progresses to cardiac dilatation and fibrosis with age.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal echocardiography and histology data shown in Figures 2, 3.

claim: Lack of MKK6 blunts p38α activation while causing MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperphosphorylation and increased mTOR signaling, resulting in cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Mechanistically, lack of MKK6 blunts p38α activation while causing MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperphosphorylation and increased mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling, resulting in cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot analysis and functional studies shown in Figures 5, 7.

claim: Cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice is reverted by knocking out either p38γ or p38δ.
source: Cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice is reverted by knocking out either p38γ or p38δ or by inhibiting the mTOR pathway with rapamycin.
evidence: Supported by heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: Cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice is reverted by inhibiting the mTOR pathway with rapamycin.
source: Cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice is reverted by knocking out either p38γ or p38δ or by inhibiting the mTOR pathway with rapamycin.
evidence: Supported by heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements after rapamycin treatment shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: The MKK3/6-p38γ/δ pathway plays a key role in the development of cardiac hypertrophy.
source: In conclusion, we have identified a key role for the MKK3/6-p38γ/δ pathway in the development of cardiac hypertrophy
evidence: Inferred from the collective findings showing that MKK6 deficiency leads to MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperactivation and cardiac hypertrophy.

claim: p38α inhibitors might result in cardiotoxicity in long-term treatment.
source: which has important implications for the clinical use of p38α inhibitors in the long-term treatment since they might result in cardiotoxicity.
evidence: Speculated based on the finding that loss of p38α activity leads to MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperactivation and cardiac hypertrophy.

claim: Cardiac hypertrophy is an adaptive response of the heart to hemodynamic stress that can be physiological or pathological.
source: Cardiac hypertrophy is an adaptive response of the heart to hemodynamic stress that can be physiological (e.g. pregnancy or exercise) or pathological (e.g. hypertension or valvular disease).
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about cardiac hypertrophy.

claim: Physiological cardiac hypertrophy is accompanied by a normal or even enhanced cardiac function.
source: Physiological cardiac hypertrophy is accompanied by a normal or even enhanced cardiac function, while pathological forms of hypertrophy are accompanied by myocardial dysfunction and fibrosis and represent a risk factor for ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death (Maillet et al., 2013; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maillet et al., 2013; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020.

claim: Pathological forms of hypertrophy are accompanied by myocardial dysfunction and fibrosis and represent a risk factor for ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.
source: Physiological cardiac hypertrophy is accompanied by a normal or even enhanced cardiac function, while pathological forms of hypertrophy are accompanied by myocardial dysfunction and fibrosis and represent a risk factor for ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death (Maillet et al., 2013; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maillet et al., 2013; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020.

claim: Cardiac hypertrophy is initially induced as a compensatory response to preserve cardiac function under stressful conditions.
source: Initially, cardiac hypertrophy is induced as a compensatory response to preserve cardiac function under stressful conditions, a process known as adaptive cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about cardiac hypertrophy.

claim: If the pathological stimulus is maintained, adaptive cardiac hypertrophy will eventually lead to the development of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure.
source: However, if the pathological stimulus is maintained, this adaptive cardiac hypertrophy will eventually lead to the development of pathological cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure (Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020.

claim: The form of cardiac hypertrophy developed depends on the type of the hypertrophic stimuli, the duration of the stimuli, and the downstream signaling involved.
source: The form of cardiac hypertrophy developed will depend on the type of the hypertrophic stimuli, the duration of the stimuli, and the downstream signaling involved (Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020; Shimizu and Minamino, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Oldfield et al., 2020; Shimizu and Minamino, 2016.

claim: Several signaling pathways known to promote physiological cardiac hypertrophic growth have been found to drive pathological hypertrophy and cardiac dysfunction when persistently activated.
source: Several signaling pathways known to promote physiological cardiac hypertrophic growth have been found to drive pathological hypertrophy and cardiac dysfunction when persistently activated (Heineke and Molkentin, 2006; Maillet et al., 2013; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Porrello et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heineke and Molkentin, 2006; Maillet et al., 2013; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018; Porrello et al., 2008.

claim: IGF1 or Akt transgenic mice develop proportionately enlarged hearts with initially normal cardiac function, which over time progress to pathological hypertrophy with impaired cardiac function.
source: For instance, IGF1 or Akt transgenic mice develop proportionately enlarged hearts with initially normal cardiac function, which over time progress to pathological hypertrophy with impaired cardiac function (Delaughter et al., 1999; Shiojima et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Delaughter et al., 1999; Shiojima et al., 2005.

claim: An essential feature of both physiological and pathological hypertrophy is increased protein synthesis, critically regulated by the mTOR pathway.
source: An essential feature of both physiological and pathological hypertrophy is increased protein synthesis, critically regulated by the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway mainly through the phosphorylation of its downstream substrates.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about cardiac hypertrophy and mTOR signaling.

claim: Activation of mTOR signaling is increased during postnatal cardiac development.
source: Activation of mTOR signaling is increased during postnatal cardiac development (González-Terán et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: Activation of mTOR signaling is increased in the hearts of transgenic mouse models suffering from physiological cardiac hypertrophy.
source: as well as in the hearts of transgenic mouse models suffering from physiological cardiac hypertrophy (McMullen et al., 2004a; McMullen et al., 2004b; Shioi et al., 2000; Shioi et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to McMullen et al., 2004a; McMullen et al., 2004b; Shioi et al., 2000; Shioi et al., 2003.

claim: The specific mTOR inhibitor rapamycin attenuates and reverses cardiac-overload-induced pathological hypertrophy.
source: Moreover, the specific mTOR inhibitor rapamycin attenuates and reverses cardiac-overload-induced pathological hypertrophy (Shioi et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shioi et al., 2003.

claim: Stress-inducing stimuli in the heart activate several mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) including the p38 family.
source: Stress-inducing stimuli in the heart activate several mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) including the p38 family.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about MAPK signaling.

claim: p38 kinases control a wide range of processes, and their dysregulation has been linked to numerous diseases.
source: p38 kinases control a wide range of processes, and their dysregulation has been linked to numerous diseases, making them a promising pharmacological target for therapeutic use (Canovas and Nebreda, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Canovas and Nebreda, 2021.

claim: The main p38 upstream activators are the MAPK MKK3 and MKK6, which are highly selective for p38 MAPKs and do not activate JNKs or ERK1/2.
source: The main p38 upstream activators are the MAPK MKK3 and MKK6, which are highly selective for p38 MAPKs and do not activate c-Jun N-terminal kinases (JNKs) or ERK1/2 (Cuenda et al., 1996; Cuenda et al., 1997; Dérijard et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cuenda et al., 1996; Cuenda et al., 1997; Dérijard et al., 1995.

claim: Mice lacking both MKK3 and MKK6 are non-viable and die in mid-gestation, associated with defects in the placenta and the embryonic vasculature.
source: Mice lacking both MKK3 and MKK6 are non-viable and die in mid-gestation, associated with defects in the placenta and the embryonic vasculature (Brancho et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brancho et al., 2003.

claim: Mice individually lacking MKK3 or MKK6 are healthy, indicating partial functional overlap.
source: In contrast, mice individually lacking MKK3 or MKK6 are healthy, indicating partial functional overlap (Lu et al., 1999; Tanaka et al., 2002; Wysk et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lu et al., 1999; Tanaka et al., 2002; Wysk et al., 1999.

claim: Both MKK3 and MKK6 are expressed in cardiac tissue and have been implicated in cardiac hypertrophy.
source: Both MKKs are expressed in cardiac tissue and have been implicated in cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about MKK expression and function.

claim: Evidence for MKK3 and MKK6 involvement in cardiac hypertrophy is based on overexpressing dominant negative or constitutively active mutants, which could produce artifactual phenotypes.
source: But, this evidence is based on overexpressing dominant negative or constitutively active MKK3 and MKK6 mutants, and these non-physiological models could produce artifactual phenotypes (Braz et al., 2003; Muslin, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braz et al., 2003; Muslin, 2008.

claim: It is not known which MKK is the main isoform required for activation of the different p38s family members during postnatal growth and in response to other hypertrophic stimuli.
source: Moreover, it is not known which MKK is the main isoform required for activation of the different p38s family members (p38α, p38β, p38γ, and p38δ) during postnatal growth and in response to other hypertrophic stimuli.
evidence: Identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The heart expresses all four p38s, but protein levels are higher for p38α and p38γ.
source: The heart expresses all four p38s, but protein levels are higher for p38α and p38γ (Dumont et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dumont et al., 2019.

claim: During embryonic development, p38α and p38β play redundant roles in the regulation of cardiac proliferation.
source: During embryonic development, p38α and p38β play redundant roles in the regulation of cardiac proliferation; mice lacking both kinases develop septal defects.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about p38α and p38β function.

claim: Mice lacking both p38α and p38β develop septal defects.
source: During embryonic development, p38α and p38β play redundant roles in the regulation of cardiac proliferation; mice lacking both kinases develop septal defects.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about p38α and p38β function.

claim: Mice lacking cardiac p38α or p38β alone have a normal cardiac structure and function under baseline conditions.
source: However, mice lacking cardiac p38α or p38β alone have a normal cardiac structure and function under baseline conditions (del Barco Barrantes et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to del Barco Barrantes et al., 2011.

claim: In response to cardiac overload, p38α contributes to myocyte apoptosis.
source: In response to cardiac overload, p38α contributes to myocyte apoptosis (Nishida et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Nishida et al., 2004.

claim: p38β might affect hypertrophic response in response to cardiac overload.
source: whereas p38β might affect hypertrophic response (Baines and Molkentin, 2005; Braz et al., 2003; Liao et al., 2001; Petrich and Wang, 2004; Wang, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baines and Molkentin, 2005; Braz et al., 2003; Liao et al., 2001; Petrich and Wang, 2004; Wang, 2007.

claim: p38γ and p38δ have a predominant role in the regulation of cardiac hypertrophy mediating physiological early postnatal and pathological angiotensin II-induced cardiac hypertrophy through mTOR activation.
source: We have previously shown that p38γ and p38δ have a predominant role in the regulation of the cardiac hypertrophy mediating physiological early postnatal and pathological angiotensin II-induced cardiac hypertrophy through mTOR activation (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: p38γ and p38δ control the postnatal metabolic switch in the heart blocking glycogen storage by the inhibition of GYS1.
source: Additionally, p38γ and p38δ control the postnatal metabolic switch in the heart blocking glycogen storage by the inhibition of GYS1 (Santamans et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santamans et al., 2021.

claim: There is a not previously described specificity of MKK3 for the activation of p38γ/δ and MKK6 for the activation of p38α in the heart.
source: Here, we demonstrate a not previously described specificity of MKK3 for the activation of p38γ/δ and MKK6 for the activation of p38α in the heart.
evidence: Inferred from the differential phosphorylation patterns of p38 isoforms in MKK3 and MKK6 knockout mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: MKK3/p38γ/δ hyperactivation in MKK6 KO mice promotes cardiac hypertrophy through mTOR activation.
source: Furthermore, we find that MKK3/p38γ/δ hyperactivation in MKK6 KO mice promotes cardiac hypertrophy through mTOR activation, which progresses to a pathological cardiac hypertrophy phenotype with age and development of cardiac dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by data showing MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperactivation, mTOR activation, and cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice.

claim: Cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice progresses to a pathological cardiac hypertrophy phenotype with age and development of cardiac dysfunction.
source: Furthermore, we find that MKK3/p38γ/δ hyperactivation in MKK6 KO mice promotes cardiac hypertrophy through mTOR activation, which progresses to a pathological cardiac hypertrophy phenotype with age and development of cardiac dysfunction.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal echocardiography and histology data shown in Figures 2, 3.

claim: p38α inhibits MKK3 expression and activation in the heart.
source: In addition, using mice lacking muscle p38α, we found that this kinase inhibits MKK3 expression and activation in the heart.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot and RT-qPCR data showing increased MKK3 expression and phosphorylation in p38α-deficient mice shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The two main upstream p38 activators are strongly biased toward the activation of specific p38 MAPK isoforms in the heart, with p38γ/δ mainly regulated by MKK3 and p38α by MKK6.
source: The present study provides several independent lines of evidence supporting a critical role for the MKK3/6–p38γ/δ signaling pathway in the development of cardiac hypertrophy. The cardiac hypertrophy developed in mice lacking MKK6 seems to be physiological in young animals, with normal or even increased cardiac function at baseline. However, aging induced the development of cardiac dysfunction and premature death. Extensive analysis with different knockout mouse models shows that in the absence of MKK6, the MKK3-stimulated p38γ/δ kinases become hyperactivated and induce enhanced postnatal hypertrophic growth through the mTOR pathway (Figure 8). Our results also reveal that the two main upstream p38 activators are strongly biased toward the activation of specific p38 MAPK isoforms in the heart, with p38γ/δ mainly regulated by MKK3 and p38α by MKK6, at least in homeostatic conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the differential phosphorylation patterns of p38 isoforms in MKK3 and MKK6 knockout mice.

claim: The cardiac hypertrophy developed in mice lacking MKK6 seems to be physiological in young animals, with normal or even increased cardiac function at baseline.
source: The cardiac hypertrophy developed in mice lacking MKK6 seems to be physiological in young animals, with normal or even increased cardiac function at baseline.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data showing normal or increased cardiac function in 9-week-old MKK6 KO mice shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Aging induces the development of cardiac dysfunction and premature death in MKK6 KO mice.
source: However, aging induced the development of cardiac dysfunction and premature death.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in aged mice and survival data shown in Figures 1E, 2.

claim: In the absence of MKK6, the MKK3-stimulated p38γ/δ kinases become hyperactivated and induce enhanced postnatal hypertrophic growth through the mTOR pathway.
source: Extensive analysis with different knockout mouse models shows that in the absence of MKK6, the MKK3-stimulated p38γ/δ kinases become hyperactivated and induce enhanced postnatal hypertrophic growth through the mTOR pathway (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by data showing MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperactivation, mTOR activation, and cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice, and rescue by p38γ/δ deletion or rapamycin treatment.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active or dominant negative forms of MKK3/6 in vitro results in cardiac hypertrophy.
source: For instance, either overexpression of constitutively active or dominant negative forms of MKK3/6 in vitro result in cardiac hypertrophy (Braz et al., 2003; Streicher et al., 2010; Zechner et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to Braz et al., 2003; Streicher et al., 2010; Zechner et al., 1997.

claim: In vivo transgenic overexpression of MKK6 in mouse heart did not affect cardiac hypertrophy but resulted in protection against myocardial infarction and reduced levels of markers of apoptosis.
source: while in vivo transgenic overexpression of MKK6 in mouse heart did not affect cardiac hypertrophy but resulted in protection against myocardial infarction and reduced levels of markers of apoptosis (Martindale et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martindale et al., 2005.

claim: MKK3 activity promotes hypertrophic growth.
source: Our in vivo data support a model wherein MKK3 activity promotes hypertrophic growth.
evidence: Inferred from the cardiac hypertrophy observed in MKK6 KO mice with MKK3 hyperactivation and the smaller hearts in MKK3 KO mice.

claim: MKK3 hyperactivation resulting from MKK6 deletion leads to cardiac hypertrophy.
source: We show that MKK3 hyperactivation resulting from MKK6 deletion leads to cardiac hypertrophy, while MKK3 genetic ablation results in reduced postnatal cardiac growth.
evidence: Supported by data showing cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice with MKK3 hyperactivation shown in Figures 3, 5.

claim: MKK3 genetic ablation results in reduced postnatal cardiac growth.
source: We show that MKK3 hyperactivation resulting from MKK6 deletion leads to cardiac hypertrophy, while MKK3 genetic ablation results in reduced postnatal cardiac growth.
evidence: Supported by heart weight measurements in MKK3 KO mice shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Deficiency of MKK6 in cardiomyocytes is sufficient to result in cardiac hypertrophy.
source: We also demonstrate that deficiency of MKK6 in cardiomyocytes is sufficient to result in cardiac hypertrophy, attributable to both, MKK6 direct function in inducing hypertrophy via p38-mediated signaling as well as its role as a negative regulator of MKK3 activity.
evidence: Supported by cardiac hypertrophy phenotype in cardiomyocyte-specific MKK6 knockout mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: MKK6 has a direct function in inducing hypertrophy via p38-mediated signaling.
source: We also demonstrate that deficiency of MKK6 in cardiomyocytes is sufficient to result in cardiac hypertrophy, attributable to both, MKK6 direct function in inducing hypertrophy via p38-mediated signaling as well as its role as a negative regulator of MKK3 activity.
evidence: Inferred from the cardiac hypertrophy phenotype in MKK6-deficient mice and the role of p38 signaling.

claim: MKK6 has a role as a negative regulator of MKK3 activity.
source: We also demonstrate that deficiency of MKK6 in cardiomyocytes is sufficient to result in cardiac hypertrophy, attributable to both, MKK6 direct function in inducing hypertrophy via p38-mediated signaling as well as its role as a negative regulator of MKK3 activity.
evidence: Supported by increased MKK3 phosphorylation in MKK6 KO mice shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The negative regulation of MKK3 by MKK6 is mediated by p38α, both at the expression and the phosphorylation level of MKK3.
source: Our results indicate that this negative regulation is mediated by p38α, both at the expression and the phosphorylation level of MKK3.
evidence: Supported by increased MKK3 expression and phosphorylation in p38α-deficient mice shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: p38α might negatively regulate the MKK3/6 upstream kinase MAP3K TAK1.
source: Additionally, there is evidence indicating that p38α might negatively regulate the MKK3/6 upstream kinase MAP3K TAK1 (Singhirunnusorn et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singhirunnusorn et al., 2005.

claim: In other tissues, the lack of p38α induces p38γ and p38δ activation.
source: Indeed, we have found that in other tissues, the lack of p38α induces p38γ and p38δ activation (Matesanz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matesanz et al., 2018.

claim: The negative feedback activity of p38α is consistent with MKK3 hyperphosphorylation identified in MKK6 KO mice and in p38αMCK-KO mice.
source: The negative feedback activity of p38α is consistent with MKK3 hyperphosphorylation identified in MKK6 KO mice and in p38αMCK-KO mice.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data showing increased MKK3 phosphorylation in MKK6 KO and p38αMCK-KO mice shown in Figures 5C, 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MKK3 preferentially regulates p38γ and p38δ activation.
source: Our results provide the first demonstration that MKK3 preferentially regulates p38γ and p38δ activation, whereas MKK6 is responsible for p38α regulation.
evidence: Inferred from the differential phosphorylation patterns of p38 isoforms in MKK3 and MKK6 knockout mice shown in Figure 5.

claim: MKK6 is responsible for p38α regulation.
source: Our results provide the first demonstration that MKK3 preferentially regulates p38γ and p38δ activation, whereas MKK6 is responsible for p38α regulation.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced p38α phosphorylation in MKK6 KO mice shown in Figure 5B.

claim: MKK6-deficient mice show p38γ/δ hyperactivation and impaired p38α activation.
source: MKK6-deficient mice show p38γ/δ hyperactivation and impaired p38α activation, possibly implicating any of these isoforms in the observed phenotypes.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and immunoblot data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: Hyperphosphorylated MKK3 promotes cardiac hypertrophic growth through activation of p38γ/δ-DEPTOR-mediated mTOR signaling in the heart.
source: Through the use of multiple in vivo models, we show that hyperphosphorylated MKK3 promotes cardiac hypertrophic growth through activation of p38γ/δ-DEPTOR-mediated mTOR signaling in the heart.
evidence: Supported by data showing MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperactivation, DEPTOR reduction, mTOR activation, and cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice, and rescue by p38γ/δ deletion or rapamycin treatment.

claim: p38α does not mediate hypertrophic responses in animal models of pressure-overload cardiac hypertrophy.
source: This is consistent with our earlier work showing an essential role for these p38 isoforms in mTOR-dependent physiological and pathological cardiac hypertrophy (González-Terán et al., 2016), as well as with previous reports indicating that p38α does not mediate hypertrophic responses in animal models of pressure-overload cardiac hypertrophy (Nishida et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nishida et al., 2004.

claim: The reversion of cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6-deficient mice also deficient for cardiac p38γ or p38δ corroborates that p38γ/δ mediate cardiac hypertrophy.
source: This conclusion is corroborated by the reversion of cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6-deficient mice also deficient for cardiac p38γ or p38δ
evidence: Supported by heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements in double knockout mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: The ability of the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin to prevent cardiac hypertrophy during early postnatal cardiac development in MKK6-deficient mice corroborates that mTOR mediates cardiac hypertrophy.
source: and further corroboration comes from the ability of the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin to prevent cardiac hypertrophy during early postnatal cardiac development in MKK6-deficient mice.
evidence: Supported by heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements after rapamycin treatment shown in Figure 7E-G.

claim: Impaired p38γ and p38δ activation and reduced postnatal hypertrophic growth in MKK3-deficient mice correlate with the findings in MKK6-deficient mice.
source: These findings correlate with impaired p38γ and p38δ activation and reduced postnatal hypertrophic growth in MKK3-deficient mice.
evidence: Supported by immunoprecipitation and heart weight data in MKK3 KO mice shown in Figure 5D, E.

claim: Apart from mTOR activation, MKK6 deficiency might affect other signaling pathways affecting cardiac hypertrophy.
source: This result suggests that, apart from mTOR activation, MKK6 deficiency might affect other signaling pathways affecting cardiac hypertrophy.
evidence: Inferred from the incomplete rescue of cardiac hypertrophy in MKK3/6 double knockout mice shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3C.

claim: p38γ/δ have been implicated in the regulation of the postnatal cardiac metabolism.
source: For example, p38γ/δ have been implicated in the regulation of the postnatal cardiac metabolism (Santamans et al., 2021), which is another known direct cause of cardiac hypertrophy (Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Santamans et al., 2021 and Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018.

claim: Cardiac metabolism is a known direct cause of cardiac hypertrophy.
source: For example, p38γ/δ have been implicated in the regulation of the postnatal cardiac metabolism (Santamans et al., 2021), which is another known direct cause of cardiac hypertrophy (Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018.

claim: The p38γ- and p38δ-mediated control of cardiac hypertrophy during postnatal cardiac development resides in cardiomyocytes.
source: The p38γ- and p38δ-mediated control of cardiac hypertrophy during postnatal cardiac development resides in cardiomyocytes (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: Lack of MKK6 in skeletal muscle or cardiomyocytes yields the same phenotype as global MKK6 deficiency.
source: Accordingly, lack of MKK6 in skeletal muscle or cardiomyocytes yields the same phenotype as global MKK6 deficiency.
evidence: Supported by cardiac hypertrophy phenotype in cardiomyocyte-specific MKK6 knockout mice shown in Figure 4.

claim: The blockade of cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6-deficient mice upon deletion of p38δ specifically in striated muscle indicates that cardiac p38δ lies downstream of MKK6 in the signaling pathway controlling hypertrophic growth.
source: Furthermore, the blockade of cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6-deficient mice upon deletion of p38δ specifically in striated muscle indicates that cardiac p38δ lies downstream of MKK6 in the signaling pathway controlling hypertrophic growth.
evidence: Supported by heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements in MKK6 KO/p38δMCK-KO mice shown in Figure 6D-F.

claim: Reversion of the MKK6-deficient phenotype upon p38δ deletion is greater than that achieved upon deletion of p38γ.
source: Interestingly, reversion of the MKK6-deficient phenotype upon p38δ deletion was greater than that achieved upon deletion of p38γ (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by comparison of heart weight and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area measurements in MKK6/p38γ DKO and MKK6 KO/p38δMCK-KO mice shown in Figure 6.

claim: p38δ has a dominant role in regulating cardiac hypertrophic growth.
source: consistent with the reported dominance of p38δ in regulating cardiac hypertrophic growth (González-Terán et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Terán et al., 2016.

claim: Young MKK6-deficient mice develop a cardiac hypertrophy that could be classified as physiological.
source: Young MKK6-deficient mice develop a cardiac hypertrophy that could be classified as physiological, characterized by a proportionate increase in heart size with the maintenance of a normal cardiac structure.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography and histology data in 9-week-old MKK6 KO mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: Physiological cardiac hypertrophy is characterized by a proportionate increase in heart size with the maintenance of a normal cardiac structure.
source: Young MKK6-deficient mice develop a cardiac hypertrophy that could be classified as physiological, characterized by a proportionate increase in heart size with the maintenance of a normal cardiac structure.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about physiological cardiac hypertrophy.

claim: Cardiac function in young MKK6-deficient mice is normal, with increased cardiac output and stroke volume.
source: Moreover, cardiac function was normal, with increased cardiac output and stroke volume, and there was no evidence of fibrosis or re-expression of the cardiac stress fetal gene program.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There is no evidence of fibrosis or re-expression of the cardiac stress fetal gene program in young MKK6-deficient mice.
source: Moreover, cardiac function was normal, with increased cardiac output and stroke volume, and there was no evidence of fibrosis or re-expression of the cardiac stress fetal gene program.
evidence: Supported by histology and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C, D.

claim: Physiological cardiac hypertrophy is an adaptive response that increases ventricular mass while maintaining or enhancing cardiac function.
source: Physiological cardiac hypertrophy is an adaptive response that increases ventricular mass while maintaining or enhancing cardiac function (Kang, 2006; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kang, 2006; Nakamura and Sadoshima, 2018.

claim: Sustained activation of the pathways that drive physiological cardiac hypertrophy can ultimately result in pathological remodeling and associated sudden cardiac death.
source: However, it has increasingly become appreciated that sustained activation of the pathways that drive this beneficial response can ultimately result in pathological remodeling and associated sudden cardiac death (Condorelli et al., 2002; Lauschke and Maisch, 2009; Matsui et al., 2002; McMullen et al., 2004a; Oldfield et al., 2020; Shioi et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Condorelli et al., 2002; Lauschke and Maisch, 2009; Matsui et al., 2002; McMullen et al., 2004a; Oldfield et al., 2020; Shioi et al., 2002.

claim: The cardiac hypertrophy observed in MKK6 KO mice becomes deleterious with age, compromising the cardiac function.
source: In agreement with this, the cardiac hypertrophy observed in MKK6 KO mice becomes deleterious with age, compromising the cardiac function, and likely contributing to the reduced survival observed in these mice.
evidence: Supported by echocardiography data in aged mice and survival data shown in Figures 1E, 2.

claim: The cardiac hypertrophy observed in MKK6 KO mice likely contributes to the reduced survival observed in these mice.
source: In agreement with this, the cardiac hypertrophy observed in MKK6 KO mice becomes deleterious with age, compromising the cardiac function, and likely contributing to the reduced survival observed in these mice.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between cardiac dysfunction and premature death in MKK6 KO mice.

claim: Cardiac dysfunction due to the deficiency of MKK6 restricted to cardiomyocytes results in a reduced lifespan.
source: We corroborated that cardiac dysfunction due to the deficiency of MKK6 restricted to cardiomyocytes in conditional KO mice also resulted in a reduced lifespan.
evidence: Supported by survival data in MKK6αMHC-KO mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Dysfunction of other organs may also contribute to the premature death of MKK6 KO mice.
source: Nevertheless, it cannot be discarded that dysfunction of other organs may also contribute to the premature death of MKK6 KO mice.
evidence: Speculated based on the whole-body phenotype of MKK6 KO mice.

claim: Respiratory weakness related to kyphosis or ataxia could contribute to the reduced survival of MKK6 KO mice at advanced ages.
source: Respiratory weakness related to kyphosis or ataxia could also contribute to the reduced survival of these mice at advanced ages.
evidence: Speculated based on the kyphosis and ataxia phenotypes observed in MKK6 KO mice.

claim: Cardiomyopathy and heart dysfunction play an important role in disease progression in Duchenne muscular dystrophy or Huntington's disease, and it is the leading cause of death in patients.
source: This would be in line with the phenotypic alterations observed in other disease mouse models with reduced lifespan, such as Duchenne muscular dystrophy or Huntington's disease, in which cardiomyopathy and heart dysfunction play an important role in disease progression, and it is the leading cause of death in patients (Burns et al., 2015; Caravia et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burns et al., 2015; Caravia et al., 2018.

claim: The activation of the p38α pathway has been linked to several diseases.
source: The activation of the p38α pathway has been linked to several diseases, suggesting that this pathway could represent a target for their treatment.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about p38α signaling.

claim: The results from clinical trials with p38α inhibitors have been disappointing so far.
source: However, the results from the clinical trials have been disappointing so far (Canovas and Nebreda, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Canovas and Nebreda, 2021.

claim: Studies with p38α inhibitors usually do not consider the possible undesired effect of p38α inhibition upon the other p38 pathway kinases.
source: However, these studies usually do not consider the possible undesired effect of p38α inhibition upon the other p38 pathway kinases, which could be among the reasons for failure in the outcomes.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings of the study.

claim: p38α inhibition leads to an unexpected activation of MKK3-p38γ/δ axis, having deleterious effects on the heart in the long term.
source: Our results show an example of how p38α inhibition leads to an unexpected activation of MKK3-p38γ/δ axis, having deleterious effects on the heart in the long term.
evidence: Inferred from the findings showing that loss of p38α activity leads to MKK3-p38γ/δ hyperactivation and cardiac hypertrophy.

claim: Treatment strategies using longstanding p38α inhibition should consider the potential cardiovascular risk among the possible secondary effects of the treatment.
source: Our finding suggests that treatment strategies using longstanding p38α inhibition should consider the potential cardiovascular risk among the possible secondary effects of the treatment.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings of the study showing cardiac hypertrophy and dysfunction in MKK6 KO mice.

claim: Inhibition of p38γ/δ could be a therapeutic strategy to treat pathologies such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
source: Additionally, our results indicate that inhibition of p38γ/δ could be a therapeutic strategy to treat pathologies such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that still remains unexplored due to the lack of specific inhibitors for these p38 family members.
evidence: Speculated based on the findings showing that p38γ/δ deletion rescues cardiac hypertrophy in MKK6 KO mice.

claim: The lack of specific inhibitors for p38γ/δ has left the therapeutic potential of inhibiting these kinases unexplored.
source: Additionally, our results indicate that inhibition of p38γ/δ could be a therapeutic strategy to treat pathologies such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that still remains unexplored due to the lack of specific inhibitors for these p38 family members.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about the availability of p38 inhibitors.
